articles.title: La era de LeBron, la mejor de NBA 2K27 si quieres llevar a tu franquicia de la nada a lo más alto
articles.standfirst: Las épocas en NBA 2K27 han sido una de las grandes novedades del videojuego
articles.summary: Las épocas en NBA 2K27 han sido una de las grandes novedades del videojuego
articles.body: Uno de los juegos más vendidos de este año ha sido el NBA 2K27, el videojuego de baloncesto que, una vez más ha unido a gamers y amantes de este deporte. Y una de las grandes novedades que hemos visto en esta edición del NBA 2K ha sido la de las eras, es decir, que podemos viajar al pasado para jugar en las diferentes épocas de la NBA, tanto en el modo Mi Carrera como en diferentes modalidades en las que tomamos las riendas de una franquicia. Personalmente estos son unos de los mejores modos de NBA 2K, tanto MyGM como MiNBA, ya que me resulta apasionante coger las riendas de una franquicia como propietario o general manager e intentar llevarla a la gloria. Pues bien, como decíamos antes, ahora podemos llevar a cabo este trabajo en diferentes épocas de la historia de la NBA. Pero antes de hablar de las eras y de cuál es mi favorita, vamos a hablar sobre en qué consiste una reconstrucción. En estas, tomamos el mando en una franquicia y tomamos casi todas las decisiones que tienen que ver con la gestión, jugadores y hasta estilo de juego. Y algo muy positivo es que podemos elegir hasta donde llega nuestra actuación, pues, no lo vamos a negar, hay trabajos que se hacen un poco pesados. Ya sabiendo esto es importante saber qué objetivos queremos porque hay muchas formas de afrontar este modo de juego, ya directamente desde la selección del equipo. Podemos elegir a nuestro equipo favorito para tener ese vínculo personal, también escoger una de las franquicias dominantes para agrandar su leyenda o, mi favorita, seleccionar a uno de los peores equipos de la liga, para, mediante el draft y la construcción de estrellas, llevarlo hasta lo más alto, un reto más complicado y bonito. Ahora vamos con las eras, la gran novedad en este NBA 2K27. Y es que 2K ha dividido la historia de la NBA, por lo menos la más reciente que es sobre la que más conocemos, en las que podremos desarrollar nuestra historia. La primera es la de 'Magic contra Bird', que arranca en 1984 y en la que tenemos al Michael Jordan rookie. Por esto, la siguiente era es la de Jordan, que arranca en 1991 y termina en 2003, cuando arranca la era de Kobe, en la que tenemos la llegada de LeBron James a la liga y todo el éxito de los Lakers. La que viene después es, obviamente, la de LeBron, que tiene su inicio en 2010 y se caracteriza por la llegada de los superequipos hasta que comienza la era de Curry, que empieza en 2016. Y para finalizar tenemos la época actual, la que empieza desde esta misma temporada 2026/27. Pues bien, una vez presentadas todas te explico por qué la era de LeBron es la mejor para coger las riendas de una franquicia. Lo primero de todo es que las normas de la liga y los límites salariales son parecidos a los que tenemos en la actualidad, así que no nos tendremos que 'romper la cabeza' cada vez que acudamos a la agencia libre o tengamos que hacer renovaciones. Pero lo más importante es que es la mezcla perfecta entre historia y actualidad. Las anteriores eras a muchos se nos quedan muy lejanas y casi todos los jugadores que en ellas triunfan o llegan a la liga ya son historia, las posteriores son demasiado cercanas a la actualidad y no cuentan mucha historia, por eso, la de LeBron, es el punto medio perfecto. Y es que a partir de 2010 llegan a la NBA jugadores que en la actualidad son estrellas en el final de su carrera, ya veteranos a los que hemos visto triunfar durante años y que podemos tener en nuestras franquicias desde que llegan a la liga, convirtiéndolos en nuestros jugadores franquicia. Y es que algo muy especial ver jugadores a los que hemos admirado tanto durante años forjarse una carrera bajo nuestro escudo. Como decía antes al inicio del artículo, uno de los puntos claves para una de mis reconstrucciones es tener un equipo malo para elegir en el draft las estrellas del futuro, por eso tiene tanto peso el draft en mis partidas y, por eso, la era de LeBron es la que más me gusta. Vamos a hacer un repaso por los drafts que entran en esta era, por lo menos de los primeros años que son los importantes. Empezamos con el primero de todos, el draft de 2011, en el que podemos seleccionar a leyendas como Kawhi Leonard, Kyrie Irving o Jimmy Butler para empezar nuestra reconstrucción. En el de 2012 para seguir apostando por el futuro nos encontramos con unos jovencísimos Anthony Davis, Bradley Beal o Damian Lillard. En el draft de 2013 un nombre destaca por encima del resto, el de Giannis Antetokounmpo, en 2014 podremos elegir a dos futuros MVPs de la liga como Nikola Jokic y Joel Embiid y en 2015 a nombres como Karl-Anthony Towns, Kristaps Porzingis o Devin Booker. Y ahora, viendo esto, ya me han entrado ganas de nuevo de probar suerte para ver a cuántas de estas estrellas puedo juntar en mi equipo. Pero esto no es todo, claro, una gran ventaja que tiene esta era es que podemos encontrar 'chollos' en el draft, ya que hemos visto su potencial y en qué se han convertido cada uno de los jugadores, por tanto, en posiciones más altas podemos encontrar a futuras estrellas como Kemba Walker, Khris Middleton, Rudy Gobbert, C.J. McCollum o Aaron Gordon. Ahora sabiendo todo esto, te voy a dar seis opciones de equipos perfectos para llevar a cabo estas reconstrucciones, franquicias que cuando comienza la era de LeBron son bastante malas y que tienen mucho potencial para crecer vía draft y también haciendo traspasos. Estas son Philadelphia 76ers, Charlotte Bobcats, Milwaukee Bucks, Cleveland Cavaliers, Detroit Pistons y Phoenix Suns.

articles.title: Aaron Ashby is on a historic heater
articles.summary: The Brewer lefty is operating in rare air
articles.body:
Aaron Ashby did not have his best season in 2026. He pitched a ton: he tied for sixth in the league in appearances, and only Houston's AJ Blubaugh surpassed his 87 bullpen innings this season (Ashby added another 2 1/3 innings in one appearance as an opener). Ashby's 89 1/3 total innings are his most in a season since 2022, when he was primarily a starter; he'd only thrown 95 innings in the big leagues total since a shoulder injury cost him the entire 2023 season. That much action — arguably overuse — sapped Ashby's effectiveness a little bit from 2025, when he was one of the best relievers in baseball:

2025: 66 2/3 innings, 2.16 ERA, 2.70 FIP, 1.170 WHIP, 10.3 K/9, 3.2 BB/9

2026: 89 1/3 innings, 3.12 ERA, 3.11 FIP, 1.310 WHIP, 11.7 K/9, 4.1 BB/9

Ashby was evolving, though, and underlying metrics suggest he wasn't actually a lesser pitcher in 2026 despite more walks and a slight downturn in results. His "Stuff+" metrics, which attempt to put a number on how "nasty" a pitcher is, mostly held in 2026; his sinker and slider, two of the best pitches in the majors in 2025, were a little worse, but his curveball and changeup were both a little better. His Statcast profile in 2026 shows just as much red as it did in 2025; in both seasons, Ashby ranked among the elite in ground ball percentage and barrel percentage. In 2026, Ashby was in at least the 88th percentile in all of expected batting average, expected ERA, whiff percentage, and strikeout percentage — all higher than last season. His average fastball velocity was up a tick, from 97.4 to 97.7 mph.

So, while Ashby's ERA was a run higher and an increase in walks created occasional problems, Ashby's stuff was just as good as it was the previous season, in about 40% more innings. Watching Ashby was not always a comfortable experience this season — his command would come and go, and his 10.7% walk rate was higher than in any previous season — but his pitches were essentially as hard to hit as ever.

Maybe it should not have been a surprise, then, what we have seen from Ashby in the postseason.

Ashby pitched in three of four games against the Padres in the NLDS. He went multiple innings in two of those three outings, and picked up a win in the Game 4 series clincher when he went three scoreless, hitless innings to bridge the game from starter Robert Gasser to the big guns at the back of the bullpen, Abner Uribe and Trevor Megill. In those three games in total, he pitched 5 2/3 innings, allowed two hits and two walks, didn't allow a run, and struck out five.

In the sweep of the Dodgers, Ashby also pitched in three of four games. In a tight Game 1, Ashby pitched the seventh and eighth in a one-run game and allowed only a walk. He picked up saves in Games 2 and 4, and his Game 4 performance — he pitched the final three innings, and twice, with the tying run on third with one out, got out of the jam — will go down in Brewers lore. His full numbers against the Dodgers: 6 2/3 innings, two hits, one walk, six strikeouts.

Through two series, Ashby has pitched in six of Milwaukee's eight games. He has totaled 12 1/3 innings; he has a win, two saves, he's allowed four hits, three walks, and no runs, and he's struck out 11.

This run is getting into historic territory. There's a whole other series to go, and who knows what will happen, but: there have been only 26 instances in the history of the postseason where a pitcher went at least 12 innings with an ERA below 1.00. If you want to drop the ERA down to zero, where Ashby's currently sits, there are only six others:

Ken Dayley, who pitched 12 shutout innings in nine appearances for the 1985 Cardinals

Mariano Rivera, twice, in the Yankees' World Series runs in 1998 and 1999

Another Yankee, Hall of Famer Goose Gossage, in 1981, who had six saves in 14 1/3 innings

Cody Allen, during Cleveland's run which ended in their Game 7 loss to the Cubs in 2016, had 10 scoreless appearances that totaled 13 2/3 innings and six saves

Finally, a surprising name: John Rocker, who didn't allow an earned run in 13 innings in the 1999 postseason (but who did allow two unearned runs)

Ashby is already at or near the innings pitched totals of all of these guys. He's in relief ace territory at this point, and there's a real argument that he should've won NLCS MVP; the cinematic nature of Jake Bauers' exploits in the series probably clinched it for him, but Ashby was certainly just as deserving.

Ashby's work in this postseason so far reminds me of two other players from the not-so-distant past. The first was another well-regarded prospect who didn't work out as a starter but who became, briefly, a shutdown reliever and a major figure of the postseason: Andrew Miller. By the time he was 26, Miller had been a top 10 prospect; he'd already thrown almost 300 big-league innings in a variety of roles, and he'd been traded twice — once as the linchpin of one of the biggest trades of the 2000s, when the Tigers traded him and others for Miguel Cabrera and Dontrelle Willis. Miller struggled as a starter but finally found success in his seventh season when he became a full-time reliever; over the next five years, Miller was as good as any relief pitcher in baseball and played a major role on several postseason teams. The 2016 campaign was the most magical, though: in 19 1/3 innings across 10 appearances for Cleveland, Miller allowed three runs (a 1.40 ERA), struck out 30 batters, and walked only five. For his entire postseason career, Miller allowed just four runs in 38 2/3 innings, giving him a lifetime 0.93 postseason ERA.

The other player I'm reminded of is Wade Davis, yet another big-time prospect who failed as a starter but who finally clicked as a full-time reliever. Davis was drafted by the Rays, but it didn't work out there; he was traded to Kansas City in the James Shields trade, but had a disastrous 2013 season as a starter. In 2014, the Royals put him in the bullpen… and over the next four seasons, Davis had a 1.45 ERA in almost 250 innings. In the 2014 postseason, Davis allowed one earned run and struck out 20 in 14 1/3 innings across 12 appearances as a setup man, including 10 innings of a 0.00 ERA across the ALCS and World Series. The following season, when Kansas City won it all, Davis did not allow a run in eight appearances; he struck out 18 and walked three in 10 2/3 innings, the Royals won every game he pitched in, and he earned four saves and a win.

From a storyline standpoint, I remember Davis and Miller dominating the postseason discussion for those three years in the mid-2010s. The idea that the role of starting pitchers in the postseason was diminishing was still quite new at the time, so it was a big deal that you had these guys coming in and mowing everybody down. They just felt like the most dangerous weapons in their respective playoff runs. Miller came up a game short (and indeed, two of the three runs that Miller gave up in that 2016 postseason run came in the Cubs' Game 7 triumph), but Davis is forever etched into the history of Kansas City baseball.

Ashby might already be there for the Brewers; even if things don't go particularly as planned in the World Series, few will forget his heroics in the first two rounds. But for a guy who, like Miller and Davis, didn't work out as a starter, and for a guy who had not had a good postseason career before this season (in 10 appearances across three seasons, he had a 7.71 ERA in 9 1/3 innings and as many walks as strikeouts), Ashby has written himself into the Milwaukee record books. If he can keep it going in the World Series, he just might join a truly elite list of postseason relief runs, the likes of which have only been seen a handful of times.

articles.title: The Street Fighter Movie Makes a Mistake Mortal Kombat Already Learned From
articles.summary: Why are fighting game movies so scared of fighting tournaments? The Street Fighter movie is just the latest example.
articles.body:
Put on your gis and gloves, fighting fans, because Street Fighter is now in theaters. The latest attempt to adapt the venerated fighting game franchise for the big screen may not be getting off to the best start with critics, but fans of the series will likely go check it out for themselves. The film does have its positive aspects, such as the gorgeous 2D animation used for flashback sequences as well as plenty of easter eggs and fighting moves ripped right from the classic games. But as a whole, Street Fighter is too slapdash to be a fully satisfying cinematic experience, and one of the biggest reasons why is that the film doesn’t use the seemingly obvious way to structure itself.

Street Fighter is a game about a fighting tournament, and while there is technically a tournament in the film, it isn’t the main focus. In fact, the movie goes out of its way to make the tournament feel like a largely incidental part of the plot, and this hurts the movie in more ways than one. What makes this even more bizarre is that this is a mistake that Mortal Kombat already made in the 2021 reboot, but the filmmakers behind Street Fighter didn’t learn the lesson from their fellow fighting franchise. How did this happen? Let’s take a look.

Street Fighter may be the first movie in this new continuity, but it takes its cast and premise from the second game, Street Fighter II. This is a smart move, since not only is Street Fighter II the most famous game in the franchise, but the first entry is commonly considered to be a well-meaning prototype for a series that didn’t fully come together until the sequel. The movie doesn’t erase the first game though, instead incorporating the first World Warrior tournament and Ryu’s victory over Muay Thai master Sagat into the animated pre-title sequence to give us backstory for our main characters, Ryu and Ken Masters. The main plot picks up six years later when main villain M. Bison sets up a second World Warrior tournament in the hopes of enticing Ryu into the spotlight to defend his title so that Bison can steal Ryu’s Hado power — that’s the energy that powers his famous Hadoken move from the games.

The tournament draws in many notable fighters from around the world, and while you would think the tournament would take up a big chunk of the runtime, it really doesn’t. Bison puts up only a cursory front of interest in the tournament, immediately kidnapping Ryu and absconding to his lab to work on draining Ryu’s Hado power. Ken wants to become the champion to prove himself to his deceased master Gouken, but his efforts to win the tournament only make up about half of his story. Ryu doesn’t participate at all on account of being kidnapped before it starts, even though he goes through the trouble of defeating E. Honda ahead of time to take his spot in the roster. Nor does Chun-Li, who — egregiously for the film — was the only woman who competed in the game. While nearly every Street Fighter II character is present in some capacity, the film moves many of the major players to the margins of the actual tournament.

This results in a bewildering viewing experience where the tournament “begins” in the second act by jumping in after one of the fights is already over, with Guile having been eliminated off-screen by Vega. Some of the other fights are similarly skipped, and multiple rounds are decided by forfeit because a character is off doing something else for plot reasons. This makes the tournament such an afterthought that it becomes impossible to invest in the scenes that do take place during it, since it’s clear that the tournament is not a priority. It also means that we never see multiple fan favorite characters like Guile and Zangief in action aside from a pointless scene early on where a bunch of the contenders brawl in a nightclub. It’s disappointing not just because we don’t get enough fighting in our Street Fighter movie, but because the filmmakers should have known better when Mortal Kombat already suffered from this same narrative stumble.

I know it may seem like we’ve all lived several lives since the ancient times of 2021, but that was when the first of the Mortal Kombat reboot films was released. Although it did well enough financially to secure a sequel, the film was a mess on the creative side, feeling like one of the worst examples of focusing on all the wrong things when trying to launch a new franchise. Instead of an engaging story centered around beloved characters from the games participating in a fighting tournament starring champions from different realms, Mortal Kombat tried and failed to endear fans to series newcomer Cole Young and never actually featured the eponymous Mortal Kombat tournament. In fact, the villain Shang Tsung’s plan is to prevent the tournament from taking place by killing Earthrealm’s champions before it can happen. It’s a strange gambit that feels like it’s working backwards to do something different instead of just delivering on straightforward genre expectations.

Given how important the Mortal Kombat tournament is to the series mythology, the film couldn’t help but make me and many others feel like Ian Malcolm in Jurassic Park: “You do plan on having Mortal Kombat in your Mortal Kombat movie, right?” It didn’t work, and much of the fan backlash to the reboot had to do with the movie excising the tournament and making unwelcome changes to MK lore, like the infamous “Arcana” tattoos that provided champions with special powers. It’s no surprise that the much more warmly received Mortal Kombat II not only jettisoned the Arcana concept and brought in series icons like Kitana and Johnny Cage, but also made the tournament the backbone of the story. Sure, the movie may not have set the world on fire, but it was a step in the right direction for a property that hasn’t had the best luck when it comes to adaptations.

So it's all the more baffling that Street Fighter falls into such a similar trap. It’s not like the movie sets the tournament aside to fill the runtime with something really interesting or subversive; it’s just thin characters and generic action scenes hastily assembled in a way that struggles to suggest any weight or gravitas. And it's not like Street Fighter has ever been Shakespeare (although Raul Julia certainly treated it as such in the 1994 film), but the games have enough iconic personalities and cultural pedigree that there’s no reason you can’t deliver a movie with entertaining action and a functional dramatic engine, especially when a conventional tournament provides the perfect built-in narrative structure of a sports movie building up to a climactic showdown. And for all the chatter about Bison’s plans to harness Psycho Power, we don’t see him go toe-to-toe with Ryu.

Instead, Street Fighter awkwardly jams in a battle between Ryu and Akuma as its climax while shuffling Bison, who has been the antagonist for most of the film, off to make a hasty getaway for a presumed sequel. And yes, Akuma is foreshadowed as Ryu’s rival via flashbacks, and it’s said beforehand he will challenge the winner of the tournament, but that rings a bit hollow when Ryu doesn’t actually win said tournament.

Street Fighter feeling half-formed is especially disappointing because video game adaptations are having a major moment. Between the Sonic the Hedgehog films becoming smash hits, acclaimed shows based on Fallout and Castlevania, and Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil movie garnering critical praise and the biggest box office take in the series’ history, the video game curse has most certainly been broken. Even Mortal Kombat has risen from the ashes with the aforementioned Mortal Kombat II being a solid and entertaining entry. Street Fighter had all the ingredients to continue the trend, but instead places fan references and sequel teases ahead of meat and potatoes storytelling. It all leads to a weird non-ending with the heroes in a car chasing after M. Bison, who has since recruited Sagat to his cause. This sequel setup would be much less frustrating if it felt like much of consequence happened in this movie.

I say this as someone with a lot of love for the offbeat fantasy lore of games like Soulcalibur and Mortal Kombat: Most people do not play fighting games for their world-building. They want to see their favorite characters in exciting 1v1 action, and the tournament conceit provides the most sensible framework to deliver that. That’s not to say you should skimp on trying to tell an actual story with the characters involved, but structurally, can we just start with the fundamentals? We’ll see if Street Fighter does well enough to warrant another round, but if it does, it would be better for everyone if the filmmakers remembered what made this franchise popular in the first place.

Carlos Morales writes novels, articles, and Mass Effect essays. You can follow his fixations on Twitter .

articles.title: Scaling the Rocks: The Brewers look inevitable
articles.summary: Colorado Rockies news and links for Saturday, October 17, 2026
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers have an answer for everything.

They've cruised through the first two rounds of the postseason at 7-1, even overcoming a 4-0 deficit to defeat the Dodgers 6-4 in Thursday's NLCS clincher and reach the World Series for the first time since 1982.

And they're getting contributions from the entire Crew.

Jake Bauers , who battled through an 11-pitch at-bat before homering off Blake Snell in Game 3, earned NLCS MVP honors. Garrett Mitchell homered in consecutive games , David Hamilton added a Game 4 insurance homer after hitting just four during the regular season, and Aaron Ashby delivered 6.2 scoreless innings out of the bullpen during the NLCS.

Everything seems to be going Milwaukee's way.

In 2007, Colorado won 21 of 22 games, sweeping their way through the NLDS and NLCS . Like Milwaukee, the Rockies found heroes everywhere. In Game 3, Yorvit Torrealba battled through a seven-pitch at-bat before launching a go-ahead three-run homer . In Game 4, rookie Seth Smith sparked a six-run inning with a pinch-hit double , and Manny Corpas closed out the 6-4 victory.

Then came eight days off and four straight losses to Boston.

Historically, sweeping the League Championship Series hasn't guaranteed a championship. Since 1995, only four of nine teams to accomplish the feat have gone on to win the World Series. Interestingly, three of those four champions have come since 2019: Washington in 2019, Houston in 2022, and Los Angeles in 2025.

Milwaukee now faces seven days off while awaiting its AL opponent. Perhaps the extended layoff matters . Or perhaps it doesn't.

Either way, looking inevitable doesn't guarantee a championship.

The Rockies made some progress in 2026, but there's still plenty of work ahead. Scott Roche examines the decisions facing Paul DePodesta, including Kyle Freeland's uncertain future, whether to bring back Tomoyuki Sugano (菅野 智之), and how Colorado might address its starting rotation. With a potential lockout looming, the front office may have a limited window to make some important moves.

Jack O'Dowd is hitting .250 with a double, a home run and four RBI through five games, while Jared Thomas has added a homer and four stolen bases in seven games. Friday's 10-0 loss to Peoria wasn't much fun, although Konner Eaton tossed 2.0 scoreless innings with two strikeouts. Check out O'Dowd's two-run homer below, and if you're looking for more baseball, MLB is streaming most AFL games for free .

TJ Rumfield's impressive rookie season is getting some recognition beyond his work at the plate. Maddy Dickens looks at the first baseman's Gold Glove candidacy and explains why he deserves more attention in the National League Rookie of the Year conversation. Rumfield finished his rookie season hitting .300 with a .390 on-base percentage, and now he's competing with Matt Olson and Ty France for a Gold Glove.

How does Colorado's farm system stack up when looking beyond traditional statistics? J.J. Cooper evaluates all 30 organizations using Statcast-based measures of pitching quality and hitting performance. It's an interesting way to examine the underlying talent being developed throughout baseball, including the Rockies' organization.

Rockies prospect Charlie Condon gets some attention in the latest Future Projection podcast from Baseball America. Ben Badler and Carlos Collazo discuss Cleveland's impressive 2022 draft class before turning to several prospects worth watching this offseason. The conversation shifts to Condon around the 34-minute mark, offering an outside perspective on one of Colorado's most intriguing young hitters.

The Guardians and Rays received an unexpected day off after Friday's ALCS Game 4 was postponed because of weather. The game has been rescheduled for Saturday, with Game 5 moving to Sunday. Cleveland holds a 2-1 series lead as both teams adjust their pitching plans and prepare to resume play.

Petey Halpin wasn't known for his power entering the postseason, but the Guardians outfielder picked a pretty good time to show some off. David Laurila examines Halpin's game-winning home run in Game 3 of the ALCS and revisits an earlier conversation about his offensive development. After hitting just four home runs during the regular season, Halpin is giving Cleveland fans something new to appreciate.

The World Series will feature two of baseball's lower-payroll clubs, an interesting development with another round of labor negotiations approaching. The Associated Press examines what the matchup means for the ongoing debate over competitive balance, payroll disparities and a potential salary cap. With the current CBA nearing expiration, there's plenty more at stake than which team takes home the trophy.

The Brewers have gotten contributions from seemingly everyone this postseason, but William Contreras has been particularly important behind the plate and in the batter's box. Michael Baumann examines the catcher's approach during Milwaukee's NLCS clincher and how his at-bats helped keep the pressure on Los Angeles.

It's never too early to start looking ahead to the next MLB Draft. Baseball America's Carlos Collazo, J.J. Cooper and Jacob Rudner discuss the early candidates for the No. 1 overall pick in 2027, including Dylan Seward , Tomas Valincius , Brendan Lawson and Dax Whitney . With no clear favorite emerging, there's plenty to sort through before next summer.

articles.title: Former ESPN star diminishes ‘the Angel Reese effect’ compared to Caitlin Clark
articles.summary: Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream are set to host Games 3 and 4 of the WNBA Finals against the Golden State Valkyries next week, with ticket prices reportedl...
articles.body:
Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream are set to host Games 3 and 4 of the WNBA Finals against the Golden State Valkyries next week, with ticket prices reportedly hitting record levels for the franchise's first Finals home games in more than a decade.

But one longtime sports media figure isn't ready to give Reese all the credit for that demand.

Former ESPN anchor Linda Cohn said the conversation comparing an "Angel Reese effect" to the "Caitlin Clark effect" is "getting ahead of itself," arguing that Atlanta's crowd will be there for the whole team and the moment, not just one player.

Dream Move Finals Games to State Farm Arena

Atlanta's run to the Finals forced a venue change. The Dream normally play at Gateway Center Arena in College Park, which seats about 3,500 for basketball.

After working around a concert and two Atlanta Hawks games, the Dream and Hawks reached a compromise to move Games 3 and 4 to State Farm Arena, which holds roughly 17,000. Game 3 is now set for Wednesday, Oct. 21, with Game 4 on Oct. 24 at 1 p.m.

With a much bigger arena, demand followed as the get-in price for Game 3 hit $201, the highest for any WNBA Finals game on record, according to TickPick data cited by Bleacher Report .

The record-breaking ticket prices quickly sparked comparisons to Clark and the Indiana Fever, who have driven attendance and ratings records since she entered the league. Cohn, however, pushed back on that comparison in a video on X as she claimed that Reese was not the only one fueling the demand.

"Angel Reese, we all know, has become one of the biggest names in the WNBA. She's helping bring attention to the Atlanta Dream. She's done it. Now Atlanta has other outstanding players. She hasn't done this alone," Cohn said.

She pointed to Rhyne Howard, Jordin Canada, and Allisha Gray before getting to her main point.

"People are already trying to compare the Angel Reese effect with a Caitlin Clark effect. And my question is, based on what exactly? A few ticket listings?" Cohn said.

Cohn added that Clark's impact has been "extraordinary" and "well documented," pointing to crowds, TV ratings, national attention, and merchandise interest.

"Now, that's not a knock on Angel Reese or any other player for that matter. It's simply recognizing what Clark has accomplished," she said. "But if we're going to make comparisons about who's driving ticket sales, let's compare actual ticket sales. Let's compare attendance. Let's compare consistent demand over an entire season, not just a couple of finals games."

She also argued that the Finals are a draw on their own and that there is nothing to prove that Reese is the one leading to these ticket sales.

"If Atlanta sells 17,000 tickets, that's terrific, but it doesn't mean every one of those people bought a ticket solely because of Angel Reese," Cohn said. "They also bought tickets to see the Dream as a team compete for a championship. It would be their first championship."

articles.title: We Sat Down with D&D Game Designer James Wyatt to Talk Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft
articles.summary: At New York Comic Con, I got a chance to sit down with Wizards of the Coast Principal Game Designer James Wyatt to talk about the first Universes Beyond expansion for D&D.
articles.body:
Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft is less than a month away, and it already looks like it's going to be a massive expansion to the tabletop game. But there are still a lot of questions about whether this new expansion is going to lean more towards the combat-oriented approach of the MMO or just be a traditional D&D game on Azeroth.

At New York Comic Con, I got a chance to sit down with Wizards of the Coast principal game designer James Wyatt to talk about the first Universes Beyond expansion for D&D. From how he was talking about the expansion, it really does sound more like a D&D game taking place on Azeroth than trying to shove WoW's complicated mechanics and combat focus on the TTRPG.

Dungeons & Dragons: World of Warcraft Images

IGN: I know that there are a lot of people who play both WoW and D&D, and I've heard some WoW players say that this is going to get them into D&D. Does the Expansion have a good on-ramp for those players?

James Wyatt: That is not its purpose, but I think it is a fantastic on-ramp in terms of someone who's a WoW player. Sitting down to make a D&D character, you're like, "Okay, what's a Tiefling? What's a Dragonborn? And what do these classes mean?" Whereas if you have that foundation of here's the WoW species, here's the WoW classes, you know the kind of character you want to make right away. This can help you steer and make those choices as a new player. We also have a very brief introductory "What is D&D?" just in case you don't know or for people who aren't familiar with it. And we steer you to D&D Beyond in particular as a place to find resources to help you get started.

So yeah, we took this down for a playtest at Blizzard last fall in the early stages, and Blizzard employees who had signed up, they signed up blind for a playtest of something. They didn't know what.

And so some of them were like, "Woo, D&D. Yes, I love D&D." And others are like, "Okay, I've never played it before. How does this go?" And I always love playing with new players because they don't know what they're supposed to do. So they are more willing to try anything they can imagine, which to my mind is really what the game is all about.

I was just telling the story of the guy who was playing the Forsaken Warlock who decided that, because he had no lower jaw, he couldn't properly cast spells. So his first spell backfired and knocked him down the stairs. And so then he tore off his own arm and threw it at the monster.

And, awesome! That's Dungeons & Dragons in a nutshell. It's not "What buttons do I have to press?" It's "What can I imagine and how do I do that? What does it look like?"

IGN: Yeah. Speaking of the combat, I know that there's a selection of dungeons that have been poured into the game, but obviously there are just too many dungeons in World of Warcraft to bring all of them over. So why did you pick the dungeons that you picked?

Wyatt: There were a couple of factors that went into that. One of them is that we started with this section on conflicts of Azeroth, which outlines the six conflicts that really have been the driving forces behind most of the expansions of WoW and talk about how they shape the world, and how you might bring them into a campaign.

All of the dungeons, I think, tie into these themes. That was one of the things that we used as a selection criteria is, does it reflect the themes of the conflicts that we're trying to emphasize here? So that was one. I was looking at popularity ranking on some wiki as another factor, just trying to get at what Dungeons people love and what's resonant for them. We started with a much larger list, made it smaller. So then it was what can we do in the space that we have and what works for the various level ranges of characters and that sort of thing.

Dungeons and Dragons: World of Warcraft – Sample Pages

IGN: There are some people who are probably going to want to see more of the raids. I think the only raid that I saw on the list was Onyxia's Lair, I might be mistaken. But will people be able to create their own Icecrown Citadel?

Wyatt: Icecrown Citadel, we are doing as a digital download adventure. We have a separate map pack that has five double-sided poster maps that are the boss fights from Icecrown Citadel. And that comes with a code for a digital download of the Icecrown Citadel adventure. So you can play through that. But I ran Blackfathom Deeps 20 years ago. It was just downloading the map from the internet and making up stats for Nagas at the time. And so using the tools in this book, you can absolutely adapt any dungeon you want to.

IGN: I saw some people concerned that this will be too focused on combat and having prescriptive dungeons. What would you say to that?

Wyatt: I think that's kind of the opposite of what we were going for, because the beauty of D&D is that when you walk into Shadowfang Keep, you can talk to anybody you meet, you can interact with anything you can see. And so the possibilities just open up tremendously over what a developer can program into any game, no matter how much care they're putting into it, because you have a DM at the table who can improvise and decide what happens.

So the dungeons that are presented here are given a pretty light touch and it's sort of like, okay, here's the dungeon map, here's the pins in the map that mark the bosses that we know you're going to encounter at some point. And what happens in between is largely a matter of improv and that you can roll on tables to generate encounters if you want a combat encounter, but you can also do something where you're exploring the environment in a way that you can't necessarily do in the MMO.

IGN: I take it that even the adventure hooks that you have open on that page there of Dire Maul, I'm sure people can create their own adventure hooks and assign their own reputation rewards and everything like that.

IGN: So this is for people who are familiar with Dungeons & Dragons at large. This is more of a guideline of how to play a game within World of Warcraft than anything else.

Wyatt: Yes, exactly. It is a great big toolbox. I mean, that's how I describe most of the books that I work on. I don't write a lot of adventure products. I do a lot of source books, and really there's that sense of we've got character options, we've got monsters, we've got dungeons you can explore. We've got guidelines for crafting your own campaign, and we've got just a big blank slate for you to play with.

IGN: World of Warcraft's obviously an evolving game that never really sits in one place. This goes up to the beginning of Midnight. Obviously, there's going to be more stories that come out over time. Are there going to be supplemental products or will it just be like, we gave you the tools, you know the story, kind of do your own thing with it?

Wyatt: Who knows? Okay, I keep saying that if I get to do another World of Warcraft book, I might postpone my retirement a little bit in order to work on it because I had so much fun working on this, loved it so much. And that depends entirely on my relationship with Blizzard and how things go from here, but I would love to do more.

And honestly, the book doesn't spend as much time on the War Within and Midnight as it could have. There's almost nothing about Xal'atath in here. Would've loved to give her a stat block, but she didn't sort of make the cut. And I'm not sure we could give her a stat block.

IGN: She does play into that Old Gods and the Void conflict pretty heavily.

Wyatt: Yeah. There's absolutely more we can do even with the story that exists now, as well as future stories. And I'm keeping a list that will be my outline as soon as I get the go-ahead and start working in another book if that ever happens. But for now, absolutely, if those are the next expansion is all about, give me something that they might focus on.

IGN: The next expansion is going to be The Last Titan, so I assume it's going to be about the Titans.

Wyatt: Right. Well, we can tell you a little bit about the Titans in here somewhere, beginning of chapter five. And honestly, my expectation is that anybody using this book is also going to spend a lot of time on the wikis because that information is there.

So yeah, we've got lots of resources for making a character that probably is not going to change significantly. I mean, the next time they give us a new class, it would be fun to do that in another D&D book.

IGN: Tell me a little bit about working the Devourer Demon Hunter into the book.

Wyatt: Pretty much as soon as I got access to the Midnight beta, I went and made a Devourer and started playing around with it and was reading what was, again, on the wikis about it. And so we already had the Demon Hunter set up with Havoc and Vengeance and just added some more spells and some direction about how to steer your Demon Hunter in that spec. They've got their own column of spells here with all the consuming soul stuff.

IGN: How did you work the WoW classes into D&D without kind of putting a wrench in the way classes traditionally work in Dungeons & Dragons?

Wyatt: The word I keep using is, rather than translation, paraphrase, that for each class I sat down and I looked at their abilities and their talent trees and all the things they can do. And I sort of cut off around level 60, I think. I don't remember now. I'd have to look at my spreadsheets. I have spreadsheets. Nobody told me that being a writer was going to involve so many spreadsheets.

And I looked for things that are already in D&D that we want to make sure to highlight in that specialization and that class, and look for opportunities to create new spells or feats or battle master maneuvers, or anything else to help evoke the most iconic flavor things.

Talents are really fiddly in WoW and D&D mechanics are not that fiddly. We don't deal with math at such a granular scale. And so again, evoking the flavor is more important to us than reproducing the mechanics in any way.

So each specialization has a selection of feats that would be good to help you do that. There is a fundamental difference though, that if you're playing a healing spec Paladin, you are a healer as opposed to a tank spec Paladin, who is a tank.

And in D&D, no matter what Paladin and subclass you choose and what feat you choose, you're both, you're a healer and a tank. And so you're not as narrowly defined by your role. So that remains true. And if you're playing a Priest, you can be wearing more than cloth armor because we couldn't easily take something away from the Cleric class to fit, and you're still casting the spells that you expect a WoW Priest to be casting.

So all of the classes I think are a little broader and give you more range of options while still helping you focus in on the role you're supposed to be playing.

IGN: I feel like in WoW stories, characters that embody those classes follow those rules anyways where it's more broad.

Wyatt: Yeah. They keep saying Anduin is a priest and there he is in plate armor with his sword.

IGN: Yeah, he is a special Priest, isn't he? So what about the mechanics for bosses? I know you described the Litch King Arthas fight, and I progressed that fight when it was current on Heroic 25, and it was hell, with mechanics like defile where you stand in it and it gets bigger. Is it as fraught or as dangerous, or is there kind of...

Wyatt: I mean, he's challenge rating 25, where D&D characters go up to level 20. So you know, it's going to be a tough fight. It's different because D&D combats are shorter in terms of the number of things you or the boss can do in the fight because they often take long enough even at three or four rounds compared to how quickly an MMO raid battle plays out, relatively speaking. So again, that idea of paraphrase rather than translation, we're trying to evoke the feeling of that fight without reproducing it exactly. But there's a lot going on here that will feel very familiar.

IGN: Could you go in and talk Arthas out of invading Azeroth with the Scourge or sneak in and steal the Helm of Domination and put it on yourself?

Wyatt: Theoretically. You can certainly try. And that's again the beauty of it, that you can talk to anybody.

IGN: Can you tell me a little bit more about the reputation system? Why did you think that was such an important thing to work into a Warcraft tabletop game?

Wyatt: So the renown system in the Dungeon Masters guide is sort of an optional rule. It's not something that we spend a lot of time with in the base game, but it is a great tool for giving factions in the world some kind of heft, a significant impact on characters' lives.

And so given particularly the importance of the Alliance and the Horde, and also the other factions in the game, I thought it would be pretty cool to use the renown system to reflect, to give characters some investment in those factions.

But fundamentally, you start caring about the welfare of the Horde if you're fighting for the Horde, and you're getting renown with the Horde, and you're getting benefits for that devotion to them.

So it's not load bearing. You can ignore it if you want to. The campaign that I'm playing in right now, it's weird because we've time traveled. We've gone back from Midnight to Classic. And so I'm not sure any of us are fully rooted in the world yet, but I'm really curious to see how that plays out over time.

I think we might have just gotten a renown reward in our last adventure, but I can't remember for sure. So yeah, it's fun. It's a way to root characters in the world and it's not essential. In the Icecrown Citadel adventure, we do a whole separate thing for your Renown with the Ashen Verdict, which goes up more quickly than you might expect Renown to go up in the core book.

But then you can get your rings improved by Armis the Penitent as your renown increases, and you're also collecting things that can make Shadowmourne and doing all of that in the context of working through the raid once rather than working through it repeatedly.

IGN: I think that's where the friction in my head is at. Because of all the time I've spent in WoW, I associate reputation with these massive grinds.

Wyatt: Yeah. That really is the key difference that even in Icecrown Citadel, I planned it out so that you get to, I think you get to 50 just about the time you kill the Lich King.

But it's like every single encounter in the Citadel, your renown increases by one or two, which is bigger than the rate we expect for most of these factions. The general idea is, and in the DMG, we even give you a conversion. If you don't want to track renown points, you can just use character level so that by the time you're 17th level, we assume you're exalted with your home faction.

IGN: On the time travel thing you mentioned earlier, the Chromie time. So for me, in the actual video game World of Warcraft, Chromie Time always felt kind of shoehorned in as "we need to get you to end game as fast as possible." And Chromie Time was just kind of the method to do that. Why Chromie Time?

Wyatt: Well, two things going on. The first is that Chromie wrote a little introduction to the book.

Wyatt: Me too. Thank you. Where she's basically saying, "I put this book together to let you visit whatever part, basically to give you your own timeline to play in."

It's a way of expressly giving the reader permission to ignore Canon, fundamentally. That's all it is. The specific example of the campaign I'm playing in, that's our DM's concoction of, okay, the campaign I want to run is modern characters.

We started off in Silvermoon City. We've just repelled Xal'atath. We're eight characters. We've just helped support the effort to repel Xal'atath. And then suddenly the time stream changes and we're in a Silvermoon city that is run by dragons. And what has happened?

So we fight some dragons and get to safety and meet Chromie who says the time stream's gone amuck. I've got to send you back 20 years to before this to prevent whatever the Infinite Dragonflight has done to mess up the timestream. So that's the story we're playing, not essential to what's in the book.

IGN: Okay. So it's not some scheme for Chromie to become the Bronze Aspect?

Wyatt: Who knows? Maybe in your campaign.

Wyatt: It's true. She's also got little notes scattered throughout the book.

Wyatt: Not very many of them, but wherever we had space on a page, she wrote a little note. "All these King Gorducks, or is it King Gordock? Anyway, I think all Big Ogres would benefit from spending some time small."

IGN: I think they would. That's a great addition. My final question is about Forever. I know you mentioned that it came out too late to get added to the book in any meaningful way, but if somebody wanted to add the Skyborne race or add the new zones that were added in, which I think a lot of the new zones in Forever were kind of cut content that existed in vanilla anyways, like Mount Hyjal.

Wyatt: Right. Yeah. I remember seeing that big blank spot on the map because I was playing early on. Yeah. Adding a new Elven lineage is not super complicated. It might be fun for us to talk to Blizzard about maybe doing that in a D&D Beyond drop or something.

But anything else that they've added content-wise, I think the content that they're adding is very easy to just port into the D&D campaign you're playing. And again, you can do anything you want. You can go anywhere you want.

IGN: I have to ask: Would you rather play Forever or Retail?

Wyatt: I wish I had time to do both. Right now I really don't have time to do either. So I've been dabbling with forever just a little bit, but I'm anxious to... I haven't finished the Midnight storyline yet, I think. So I'm anxious to get back to that, too.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: 7 Crazy Movie Premises That Actually Worked
articles.summary: Before Whalefall, these crazy movie premises actually worked too.
articles.body:
“A young man is swallowed by a whale while searching for his father’s remains deep in the ocean.”

That is the elevator pitch for Whalefall , starring Austin Abrams (Resident Evil) and co-written by Daniel Kraus and director Brian Duffield (No One Will Save You). Set for release on October 16, the film is based on Kraus’ 2023 novel, inspired by a viral video of kayakers seemingly being swallowed by a whale . Whalefall’s central conceit is one writers and directors are challenged by, and often dream of, because it raises the questions: Can I pull this off? And how can I make this work? In other words, the absolutely bonkers premise is fertile ground for real creative risk and opportunity.

Of course, Whalefall isn’t the first or only film to take a big leap. Throughout cinema history, bold filmmakers have swung for the fences and connected. Too many for just one list, in fact. Children of Men, Groundhog Day, Parasite, The Truman Show, Tie Me Up! Tie Me Down!, Spirited Away, The City of Lost Children, The Stepford Wives, Inside Out, Poor Things, Everything Everywhere All at Once, and many more could easily have made this list. The following is a small sample of films that successfully stepped out of standard storytelling boxes.

Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964)

“Gentlemen, you can’t fight in here! This is the War Room!”

Positive that communists are poisoning the “precious bodily fluids” of the American populace, General Jack D. Ripper launches an unauthorized nuclear attack on the U.S.S.R., triggering an increasingly farcical crisis which culminates in a dunce's doomsday, an apocalypse driven by insane idiots and a Nazi.

One of cinema’s great political satires, Dr. Strangelove opened in 1964, about a year and a half after the Cuban Missile Crisis, when the world held its breath, wondering if we really were going to self-destruct. Stripping away the reasoned tones that politicians of the day used to discuss nightmare scenarios, Dr. Strangelove captures the powerless fear of a populace, and exposes geopolitics for what it so often is: utterly unhinged and stupid (possibly drunk), and treating mass casualty as if it is a child’s game to win or lose.

The film cost $1.8 million to make and earned more than $9 million at the domestic box office . Though it was shut out at the Academy Awards with four nominations and zero wins, it earned several nominations and four wins at the BAFTAs, including Best British Film and Best Film from Any Source. Upon release, reviewers were polarized: some found genius in the dark comedy, while others were disturbed by its treatment of the very real threat of nuclear war. Over time, it has become director Stanley Kubrick’s highest-rated film on Rotten Tomatoes, at 98%, and was deemed so influential that the National Film Registry selected it as one of its first 25 films in 1989. Director Michael Mann went so far as to say he wasn’t really interested in movies until he saw Dr. Strangelove. It remains a standard-bearer for satire. It captures essential truth, if not (necessarily) objective reality. As for reality, military officials criticized the film upon release, yet, coincidentally or not, made internal changes that mapped to the vulnerabilities Dr. Strangelove exposed .

In a world where sentient cartoons live alongside humans, Eddie Valiant – an alcoholic private detective with a vendetta against toons – is hired to investigate a sultry cartoon femme fatale, Jessica Rabbit, who may be cuckolding her stuttering rabbit husband, Roger. When her alleged lover is found dead, Valiant is forced to protect the unruly rabbit and drawn into a sinister toon conspiracy.

Roger Rabbit was a hit with audiences and critics alike right out of the gate, and stands at 96% on Rotten Tomatoes. Praised for its visionary storytelling, which mixes zany cartoon comedy with classic noir tropes, and for its revolutionary technical achievement, the film left viewers spellbound. Though live action and animation had been integrated before, audiences had never seen anything quite like Roger Rabbit. Bob Hoskins’ emotional performance as the detective on a redemption arc was lauded, particularly in that he was acting, essentially, with empty space for much of the film. Kathleen Turner’s rich voice cemented Jessica Rabbit as an iconic animated character.

Made for $50 million ($70 million by some estimates ), the film earned just over $350 million worldwide. It had six Academy Award nominations and three wins (plus a Special Achievement Academy Award for animation direction) and was added to the National Film Registry in 2016 . Thanks to executive producer Steven Spielberg’s negotiations, it wowed audiences by bringing together animated characters from both Warner Bros. and Disney. Along with The Little Mermaid, it also helped usher in the Disney Animation renaissance. Similar releases followed, including 1992’s Cool World, starring Brad Pitt as a human detective and Kim Basinger as a cartoon femme fatale named Holli Would, and 1996’s Space Jam, which teamed Michael Jordan with the Looney Tunes. Arguably, the film that’s come closest to capturing Roger Rabbit’s appeal is the recent Coyote vs. Acme, but, for many, nothing truly touches the 1988 classic. According to director Robert Zemeckis , Stanley Kubrick deeply appreciated the film and, while watching it, searched for the hidden “sleight of hand” movie magic that made it all come together, before ultimately realizing it was “just an incredible amount of backbreaking work” that made Roger Rabbit possible.

A suicidal man embittered by career sacrifices and disappointments, and facing ruin and jail, meets with a fledgling angel (eager to advance in his own vocation) on Christmas Eve. In order for the latter to win the promotion he wants (get his wings), he must convince the former that there’s more to life than work and material success, and that his impact on the world has been sizable and good, despite all evidence to the contrary.

Perhaps that’s a hyperbolic synopsis, but the fact is, while director Frank Capra’s holiday favorite may be considered a sentimental classic today, audiences at the time of its release seemingly weren’t ready for this unorthodox take on Christmas cheer. Though it received mixed to somewhat positive reviews (particularly praising Jimmy Stewart’s lead performance) and ultimately earned five Oscar nominations, it won no Academy Awards beyond a Technical Achievement Award and was a box-office flop. RKO, the studio that released the film, reported a $525,000 loss . But It’s a Wonderful Life did nearly gain notoriety – via controversy , when the FBI flagged it to the House Un-American Activities Committee (which was investigating potential Communist influences in Hollywood), noting anti-capitalist undertones (as the film’s banker was the most hated character). Alas, it couldn’t even get negative PR, as the committee decided not to bring the creators in to testify.

The film was largely overlooked in the decades that followed. Capra himself was taken aback , if pleasantly so, when it finally found its audience. The full story is more complex, but, effectively, a clerical fluke meant the film’s copyright lapsed in 1974 , making it cheap to run on television during the holidays, which it did for many years. The copyright situation was eventually resolved through the rights in the underlying story and music. By then, it had become a beloved standard. Distance gave viewers space to see what was always there. Audiences and critics alike recognized the special magic in the strange mix of sentimentality, whimsy, very real and deeply painful human despair, and the essential truth that we all desire to know, truly know, that our lives matter. In a 1999 essay, film critic Roger Ebert said this film belonged to a category that could withstand indefinite viewings: “Like great music, they improve with familiarity.” Years after it opened and flopped, It’s a Wonderful Life became a holiday television staple, drawing millions of viewers for its Christmas Eve broadcasts, and now holds a 94% rating on Rotten Tomatoes.

While working a bland office job, struggling street puppeteer Craig Schwartz stumbles upon a portal to actor John Malkovich’s mind, where he can experience the celebrity’s life for exactly 15 minutes before being spat back out onto the New Jersey Turnpike. He and the co-worker he’s in love with start a business charging $200 per person for a visit into the actor’s experience. Eventually, multiple characters battle to permanently take over Malkovich’s life, creating a series of betrayals, identity crises, opportunities found and then lost, and the annihilation of the self.

Charlie Kaufman’s surreal screenplay is arguably one of the biggest swings on this list. Malkovich himself initially worried it would bomb , and the script circulated Hollywood with no takers. One exec reportedly asked, “Why the f— can’t it be Being Tom Cruise?” However, director Francis Ford Coppola got the script to his daughter’s then-boyfriend, Spike Jonze, who directed it and helped get it produced. The movie opened to great acclaim, presumably stunning skeptical industry players. It has a 94% on Rotten Tomatoes, with Roger Ebert calling it “endlessly inventive,” adding that “[it] has ideas enough for half a dozen films.” Critics celebrated its inventiveness, layered themes, and ensemble performances from John Cusack, Cameron Diaz, Catherine Keener, and, of course, John Malkovich.

It cost $13 million to produce and went on to earn either $23 million or $32 million globally (depending on the source). It didn’t win any of its three Oscar nominations, but it won Best First Feature and Best First Screenplay at the Independent Spirit Awards. It appears on multiple “best of” lists, including Empire magazine ’s 500 Greatest Movies of All Time and the Writers Guild of America’s 101 Greatest Screenplays Ever Written . Like Kaufman’s other films (two of which, Adaptation and Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, nearly made this list), Being John Malkovich demonstrates what is possible when you follow even the most nonsensical threads of imagination.

A SWAT team, trapped in a hostile high-rise, must battle its way up the stairs to capture a crime lord; end of story. The Raid is unique on this list in that the plot isn’t a fit of wild imagination; rather, it has almost no plot at all. It has a premise and wall-to-wall unparalleled fight sequences. It grips the viewer and doesn’t let go for the entire runtime, leaving audiences breathless and feeling like they, too, just punched their way to victory. It’s exhilarating, near-perfect action that other films have chased for 15 years.

The Indonesian actioner cost $1.1 million to make, according to director Gareth Evans , and earned over $9 million worldwide at the box office, plus another $10 million in U.S. DVD and Blu-ray sales alone. No traditional narrative necessary. It stands at 87% on Rotten Tomatoes and performed well during its film festival run – Evans said he was “blown away” by the reception at the Toronto International Film Festival. The movie became an industry reference point, with John Wick director Chad Stahelski telling Den of Geek that directors unfamiliar with fight choreography would specifically ask for something like The Raid, among other iconic action films. Yayan Ruhian and Cecep Arif Rahman, two actors from The Raid franchise, were ultimately cast as two of Keanu Reeves’ adversaries in John Wick: Chapter 3 – Parabellum. The film is a beloved fan favorite and cultural touchstone for best-in-class hand-to-hand action.

On a trip to visit his girlfriend’s parents, a talented photographer makes a horrific discovery: a group of Obama-voting white suburbanites has found a way to use misophonia-inducing teaspoons, hypnosis, and surgery to transplant the consciousness of wealthy, older white people into young, Black kidnappees, whose own psyches are sent into a purgatorial “sunken place.”

Director Jordan Peele’s groundbreaking debut became an instant cultural phenomenon, blending social commentary with genuinely entertaining horror. The director builds real suspense, psychological terror, and tension-releasing humor into a film that lays systemic racism bare through a deeply imaginative metaphor. It has a 98% on Rotten Tomatoes, and Peele made Academy Awards history as the first Black writer to win an Oscar for Best Original Screenplay. Get Out was also nominated for Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Actor (Daniel Kaluuya). In late 2021, the WGA named the script the #1 Greatest Screenplay of the 21st Century (So Far). Financially, Get Out was a juggernaut, making $255 million worldwide on a $4.5 million budget, and breaking The Blair Witch Project’s domestic record as the highest-grossing debut film based on an original screenplay.

Director Christopher Nolan had this to say of Get Out: “How often do you get the experience of seeing something that you have no idea where it's going to go, and then it goes somewhere far more interesting than you ever imagined?"

Faced with an unexpected existential crisis, Barbie must travel from the utopia of Barbieland into the “real” world to find and soothe the unhappy person playing with her so that she can once again experience the sweet oblivion of not thinking about death, or life, or meaning… and bask in thighs free of cellulite. Ken tags along and, upon discovering patriarchy, starts an uprising when he returns to Barbieland.

The overall sentiment when Barbie debuted was that this movie absolutely should not work . Yet it surprised and delighted audiences with its mix of subversive humor (that both acknowledges and reframes Barbie’s cultural impact), standout performances from producer and star Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling (as Barbie and Ken), and an optimistic core. It inspired multiple viewings for many audience members, some of whom came to theaters decked out in celebratory pink. Doctor Strange director Scott Derrickson said the film was one of his two favorites that year, and an example of IP “treated with true brilliance,” calling it an “extraordinary movie on every level.”

Set against Oppenheimer in the summer’s race for dominance, affectionately known as Barbenheimer, the film catapulted to box office success. It was a risk for both Mattel and Warner Bros., who distributed it. They trusted co-writer and largely indie director Greta Gerwig, who’d never helmed a film this big, with an iconic but controversial doll and a $128 million budget. The bet paid off: Barbie earned a staggering $1.4 billion worldwide at the box office , holds an 88% on Rotten Tomatoes, and received eight Oscar nominations, winning Best Original Song for “What Was I Made For?” and taking home the first-ever Golden Globe for Cinematic and Box Office Achievement. Ultimately, the film’s pathos stayed with viewers. Barbie is the picture of stagnant perfection, so who better to take a messy journey where triumph lies in living the most mundane moments of a human life?

What are your favorite crazy movie premises that somehow worked? Let’s discuss in the comments!

articles.title: Bose’s new wired earbuds are simple in the best way
articles.summary: Wired earbuds are making a small comeback, and Bose is capitalizing on it — with ANC this time.
articles.body: After Apple courageously removed the headphone jack from the iPhone in 2016, most people switched to Bluetooth earbuds and never looked back. But their wired counterparts have stuck around, and their sales even went up this year after five years of decline. Part of the resurgence can be tied to the fact that they’re cool now with younger generations — following the revival of tape decks and vinyl. Celebrities have been spotted wearing them, and there’s even an Instagram account that follows the trend. Wired earbuds have real benefits. They don’t need a battery, so they’ll last longer than wireless ones that eventually die, and it’s a lot harder to lose a wired pair with a long cable than a single earbud. Now, after more than a decade, Bose has returned to the wired world, but the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are no throwbacks. [Product: Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds | The $99 Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds connect over USB-C, so they don’t need an extra dongle to work with current phones. That’s also how they can offer ANC. Because the 3.5mm or 4.4mm analog audio connector doesn’t provide enough power for active noise cancellation, most wired earbuds, from cheap off-brands to wildly expensive audiophile in-ear monitors, rely on passive isolation only. Bose’s last attempt at wired in-ears with ANC, 2013’s QuietComfort 20, had a 3.5mm jack, and their ANC relied on a rechargeable battery in the cable. The new Bose earbuds don’t need the battery pack; they can get the minimal power they need for ANC from the USB-C port. There are a few other USB-C wired headphones with active noise cancellation, but not many. There’s also the $30 Belkin SoundForm ANC Wired Earbuds, which reportedly have weak noise canceling, and Audio-Technica released a pair in Asia earlier this year. The best part of the Bose earbuds, or any wired earbuds, is that they’re simple. No need to worry about pairing them, no need to charge them, and no need to fiddle with an app. Plug them into the USB-C port on a phone or computer and they just work. [Image: The in-line remote is super basic in the best way. While the noise canceling performance doesn’t measure up to Bose’s Bluetooth earbuds (the wired earbuds have two mics per side, while the QuietComfort Earbuds have three), it’s still solid for the price. It does a great job blocking low-frequency sounds like air conditioners and low truck rumbles, but has difficulty muting conversation (with ANC on, I can’t hear our air conditioner at all, but can make out every word of my wife’s phone conversation as I write this). There’s a slight high-end hiss when the noise canceling is active, but it’s only noticeable when they aren’t playing any sound. And they sound great. Vocals are clear and bright, and bass is punchy without overwhelming other instruments. I wouldn’t mind being able to cut down the high-end brightness a bit (mainly to tame cymbal ringing), but since these don’t use an app there are no EQ options. The wired connection allows for low latency, so there’s no worry about sound and video lining up, and they support high-res audio at 24-bit/48kHz. I went back and forth between CD quality (16-bit/44.1kHz) and high-res streams of the new release of The Beatles’ Rubber Soul on Qobuz, and the high-res versions sounded a bit more open and spacious. It’s not an enormous difference, but I’d listen to the high-res version on the Bose over the CD-level stream any day. The in-line remote has three buttons that control volume, playback, and noise-canceling mode selection. They respond quickly when pressed and have a nice rubberized texture. The headphones come with three ear tip sizes and two sets of wings to find a good fit (you don’t even need to use the wings if you find them uncomfortable). I was easily able to find a comfortable combination and they stayed securely in my ears for hours. The earbuds are also IPX4 rated if there’s a light rain while you’re out or you want to use them on a run. Even with the benefits of wired earbuds, though, nostalgia can’t wipe away the frustrations. If you don’t run the 4.2-foot cable under your shirt, or coil up the excess in your jacket pocket, it catches on everything. In my short time with the Bose, the cable caught on the handle of a kitchen drawer, the edge of my keyboard, the zipper of my sweatshirt, the strap of a bag I was carrying, my pocket (when I accidentally stuffed too much of the excess in with my phone), and even the hand of a stranger who got too close to me in line at Starbucks. [Image: There are three ear tip sizes and two wings available to find the right fit. And as with any wired earbuds, there’s cable noise, as vibrations from rubbing or bumping against something travel up the cable to be heard in the earbuds. Although I will say the cable insulation is enough to minimize the effect better than cheap (and older) options. The Bose struggle with wind. The microphones for noise canceling or transparency mode pick up the wind noise, and it’s distracting — with ANC on, it cuts out the low-end whoosh decently, but the high end is still incredibly present. I found turning it off was best when it was windy outside, although that meant compromising on the noise canceling. Call quality also isn’t the best. The microphone is on the in-line remote, and it picks up a good amount of ambient sound during calls. If you regularly make calls while walking busy streets, these aren’t the earbuds for you. I’m not ready to go back to 2016 and convert back to wired earbuds. In most situations, the benefits of wireless earbuds outweigh those of wired ones, and I don’t see that changing for me. But for the ease of use, convenience of a USB-C connection, lack of lag, high-res capability, sound quality, and the fact they include ANC, the Bose are unquestionably the best affordable wired option out there. Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

articles.title: Clemson Tigers vs. Charleston Southern Buccaneers: How to Watch, Live Gamethread, TV Channels
articles.summary: Good news, Clemson remains undefeated against the bye week. Bad news, we have to watch Clemson play again. Thankfully it is Cupcake Week: Midseason Edition d...
articles.body:
Good news, Clemson remains undefeated against the bye week. Bad news, we have to watch Clemson play again. Thankfully it is Cupcake Week: Midseason Edition down in Death Valley. Not sure how this ended up happening, but for the optimists that may still be here it is a chance to ease into the back half of the schedule.

Look this is always simple, no one gets hurt and Clemson can rest starters during the second half. The rest is just an added bonus. As we've said for the last 2.5 years, we are always going to hope that the OL looks competent. I'm not expecting it, but it would be nice to see. Miami was an ugly game for a number of reasons, and if ther eis any hope at salvaging the rest of the season the Tigers have to start with a good performance today.

On defense the line has to get pressure. Yes, they should do it easily, but too often this team seems to sit on its laurels or just assume it is going to out talent the opposition. Just go win the game in the first quarter and enjoy some Gatorade on the sideline.

Hopefully we get to see a few snaps from our injured guys. Dabo has mentioned a few players are ready to get back in the action, or close to it. A little bit of game action ahead of next week against Virginia Tech would be lovely.

As always, join us in the comments below.

The Golden State Valkyries have only been in the WNBA for two seasons, and they're already four wins away from a championship. After sweeping the defending champion Las Vegas Aces in the semifinals, the Valkyries return to Chase Center on Saturday for Game 1 of the WNBA Finals against the Atlanta Dream. It's a remarkable run for a franchise that didn't even exist on the court two years ago, and the Bay Area now gets to watch its newest basketball team compete for a championship with home-court advantage.

The Dream won't be an easy final obstacle, either. Atlanta swept the New York Liberty in the semifinals and enters the Finals undefeated in the postseason, with Defensive Player of the Year Angel Reese leading the charge. But Golden State won all three regular-season meetings against Atlanta, and Gabby Williams has been playing some of her best basketball when it matters most. Neither franchise has ever won a WNBA championship, so history will be made regardless of the outcome. Valkyries fans hope this incredible run ends with a trophy coming home to San Francisco.

The WNBA Finals tip off Saturday at 12:30 p.m. PDT at Chase Center, and basketball fans across the country can tune in with Sling TV and Peacock .
